subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Starburst Galaxies
description: A quick win: understand Starburst Galaxies.

hook.text: Starburst galaxies form stars at 100 times the normal rate. They blaze with the light of trillions of young stars.

buildup.text: Most starbursts are triggered by galaxy mergers. The collision compresses gas, sparking intense waves of star formation.

discovery.text: M82, the Cigar Galaxy, is the nearest starburst galaxy. Its center glows with infrared light from millions of new stars.

twist.text: Starbursts can't last forever. They burn through gas in just a few hundred million years, then go quiet.

climax.text: Superwinds from the burst blow gas out of the galaxy entirely, shutting down future star formation.

punchline.text: A hundred times the normal rate. Brief, brilliant, and self-destructive.

quiz.question: What typically triggers a starburst in a galaxy?
options: A galaxy merger that compresses gas and sparks intense star formation
A supermassive black hole that heats all the gas at once
Dark energy accelerating the rotation of the galaxy

details.summary: Starburst galaxies are forming stars at rates 10-1,000 times higher than normal galaxies — often triggered by galaxy mergers or interactions that compress vast amounts of gas.
details.whyItMatters: Starburst galaxies reveal the most extreme mode of star formation. They were far more common in the early universe when gas was abundant and mergers frequent, shaping the galaxies we see today.
takeaways: Often triggered by galaxy mergers compressing gas
Intensely bright in infrared from heated dust

faq.question: What happens after a starburst phase ends?
faq.answer: The galaxy rapidly consumes or expels its gas through stellar winds and supernova feedback. Once the gas is gone, star formation ceases abruptly. The galaxy fades to red as its massive young stars die quickly, leaving mostly older stars.

faq.question: What are ultraluminous infrared galaxies?
faq.answer: ULIRGs are the most extreme starburst galaxies, emitting over a trillion times the Sun's luminosity — almost entirely in infrared. Most are late-stage galaxy mergers where enormous amounts of gas are compressed into compact regions.
